title: Future-in-the-Past
subtitle: Talk about something that was going to happen, seen from a point in the past.
objectives: Use was/were going to for a past plan (often one that changed or didn't happen)
Use would as a narrative future, for what happened later in a story
Use was/were about to for something on the very brink of happening
Tell the difference between the three, based on the nuance each one adds

content.intro: You already know "will" and "going to" for talking about the future from now. But when you're telling a story or describing a past situation, you often need to talk about a future that existed back then — a plan, an expectation, or something about to happen at that past moment. This is called future-in-the-past.

rules.heading: a) was/were going to + bare infinitive
rules.body:
A plan or intention that existed at a point in the past — very often, one that changed or never happened.

  • She was going to call me, but she forgot.
  • We were going to have a picnic, but it started raining.

rules.heading: b) would + bare infinitive
rules.body:
Used in narration for something that turned out to happen later — usually without any sense of the plan failing; more like fate or how the story unfolded.

  • He didn't know it yet, but this decision would change his life.
  • Little did she know that the stranger would become her best friend.

rules.heading: c) was/were about to + bare infinitive
rules.body:
Something on the very brink of happening — often interrupted by something else.

  • I was about to leave when the phone rang.
  • They were about to sign the contract when the deal fell through.

examples: He was going to study abroad, but the scholarship fell through.
She had no idea that this decision would change everything.
I was about to knock when the door opened.
We were going to sell the house, but we changed our minds.
He promised he would call as soon as he landed.
Just as I was about to give up, I found the missing file.
They were going to cancel the trip because of the weather.
She didn't know that this stranger would become her closest friend.

commonMistakes.wrong: She was going to called me later.
commonMistakes.right: She was going to call me later.
commonMistakes.why: "Was going to" is always followed by the bare infinitive, not the past form.

commonMistakes.wrong: He didn't know that this decision will change everything.
commonMistakes.right: He didn't know that this decision would change everything.
commonMistakes.why: Inside a past narrative, future-in-the-past needs "would," not "will."

commonMistakes.wrong: I was about to leaving when she called.
commonMistakes.right: I was about to leave when she called.
commonMistakes.why: "Was about to" takes the bare infinitive, not the gerund.

commonMistakes.wrong: They was going to travel next month.
commonMistakes.right: They were going to travel next month.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with was/were going to, would, or was/were about to.

items.prompt: He ___ (leave) the office when the phone rang.
items.explanation: Something interrupted right at the moment it was about to happen.

items.prompt: She had no idea that this trip ___ (change) her whole outlook on life.
items.explanation: A narrative future — what turned out to happen later.

items.prompt: We ___ (visit) the museum, but it was closed for renovation.
I ___ (call) you, but my phone died first.
Just as she ___ (open) the letter, the phone rang.
items.explanation: Interrupted at the very moment of happening.

items.incorrect: She was going to visited her grandmother, but it snowed.
answer: She was going to visit her grandmother, but it snowed.
items.explanation: "Was going to" takes the bare infinitive.

items.incorrect: He didn't realize that this mistake will cost him his job.
answer: He didn't realize that this mistake would cost him his job.
items.explanation: "Will" backshifts to "would" inside a past narrative.

items.incorrect: I were about to leave when the taxi arrived.
answer: I was about to leave when the taxi arrived.

items.incorrect: They was going to cancel the trip.
answer: They were going to cancel the trip.

exercises.title: Guided Production
exercises.instructions: Write your own sentence for each prompt. There's no single correct answer — a model answer is shown for comparison after you submit.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using “was/were going to” about a plan of yours that didn't happen.
items.modelAnswer: We were going to spend the summer in Portugal, but our plans changed.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using “would” as a narrative future, describing something that later turned out to be true.
items.modelAnswer: She had no idea, as she signed the lease, that this apartment would become her home for the next ten years.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using “was/were about to” describing an interrupted moment.
items.modelAnswer: I was about to fall asleep when I heard a strange noise downstairs.

summary: Was/were going to = a past plan, often one that changed or didn't happen.
Would = a narrative future, for what turned out to happen later, without implying failure.
Was/were about to = something on the very brink of happening, often interrupted.
This is the foundation for C1's Future Forms with Nuance, which adds the more formal was/were to and complex narrative timelines.
